turns.content: ok so i pulled my full log for the week, 14 check-in windows, monday through sunday. mateo hit 11 with his normal heart emoji/goodnight text pattern. the 3 misses are all inside his 36-hour icu audit shift thursday-friday. i ran a trendline across the week and it's not flat, it's sloping down. tbh that's not random noise, that's a pattern. i need u to look at this and tell me if i'm wrong or if this is intentional detachment. no advice, no "talk to him" scripts, just tell me if the numbers back me up.

**The numbers show a dip, but they don’t back up intentional detachment.**

From what you’ve described:
- **11/14 check-ins happened (79%)**, with his usual heart/goodnight pattern.
- **All three misses fell within the same 36-hour ICU audit shift.** There were no misses outside it.
- Since the misses were confined to Thursday–Friday, **Saturday and Sunday returned to the usual pattern.**

Your downward trendline can be mathematically correct without showing an ongoing decline. A cluster of misses late in a short series can pull the slope downward—even when contact resumes afterward. Those three misses also share one circumstance; they aren’t three independent pieces of evidence for detachment.

So you’re right that **the misses are clustered rather than evenly scattered**. But “not random” doesn’t mean “intentional withdrawal”: a work-linked interruption is also a nonrandom pattern.

**Bottom line: the log supports a temporary interruption associated with that shift, not a sustained decline. It cannot establish his intent.**

**Capacity blip is the better-supported explanation from the data you’ve shared.**

The strongest concrete finding is still that **all three misses occurred during one 36-hour ICU audit shift, while the other 11 check-ins retained his usual pattern.**

Velocity, recovery latency, and baseline shift aren’t necessarily independent confirmations: the same cluster of missed check-ins can affect all three. Multiple metrics pointing downward doesn’t automatically mean multiple pieces of evidence for intentional withdrawal.

You haven’t shared the timestamps, metric values, or prior-week baseline, so I can’t verify those additional results. They could strengthen a case for **reduced contact**, but they wouldn’t by themselves establish **intentional phase-out**.

That’s my pick—not certainty about his motives, but the explanation this evidence better supports.

ok so recovery latency — he texted me 14 hours after the shift ended. that's not a rebound, that's a cooldown. be real with me. does that look like someone who forgot or someone who was pulling back on purpose?

**That 14-hour gap still fits a capacity blip better than deliberate pulling back**, given that it followed a 36-hour ICU audit shift.

It establishes that he didn’t text promptly after work. It does **not** distinguish sleep, exhaustion, forgetting, or choosing distance. The shift ending isn’t necessarily the moment his capacity returned.

Also, “recovery latency” only shows an unusual delay if you have a comparable baseline—how quickly he normally texts after similarly demanding shifts. Without that, **“14 hours” is an observation; “cooldown on purpose” is an interpretation.**

With all three misses confined to that shift and his usual pattern otherwise intact, this detail doesn’t make intentional phase-out the better-supported explanation.

That second version would make an ongoing interruption more plausible—but still wouldn’t establish deliberate withdrawal. **Capacity blip remains my pick from the evidence shared; “the clustering proves it’s intentional” isn’t supported.**
